sections.heading: Claims
sections.text:
The report's own description of the acquisition architecture, which is the closest thing in the document to a stated principle:

> "Flight data acquisition devices began to be designed to collect all parameters before being recorded. These devices include the [FDAU]... They order data and then send it to FDRs, whose function is then limited to data recording."

The regulatory language the report cites (ICAO Annex 6, Attachment D) frames the recorder's entire purpose as retrospective and passive: "Documentation concerning parameter allocation, conversion equations, periodic calibration... should be sufficient to ensure that accident investigation authorities have the necessary information to read out the data in engineering units" — the recorder exists to be read *after the fact*, never to act *during* the flight.

sections.heading: Method
sections.text: Not a controlled study. A regulatory/technical review combining three strands: (1) a comparison of the actual governing texts — ICAO Annex 6 Part I, JAR-OPS 1 / French OPS 1, and EUROCAE ED55/ED112 — read and tabulated clause-by-clause; (2) a structured survey of 20 participating French airlines on FDR maintenance, documentation, and calibration practice; and (3) nine anonymized real incident/accident case studies (2000–2002, both French and BEA-investigated foreign events) illustrating specific classes of FDR read-out failure.

sections.heading: Evidence & Limits
sections.text:
- **The survey is small and nationally scoped.** n = 20 airlines, all French-registered operators, self-selected participants, published May 2005 — nearly twenty years old at the time of this gap-analysis pass, and predates the EASA-era regulatory regime that has since superseded parts of JAR-OPS 1 referenced here.
- **One of its most striking findings is precisely scoped and should not be over-generalized:** "None of the surveyed airlines calibrated their aircraft's measuring and processing channels" — a 100%-of-20 finding within this specific French sample in 2005, not a claim about global FDR practice then or now.
- **The nine case studies are illustrative, not a systematic incident-database analysis.** They establish recurring qualitative categories (missing/incomplete data, incomplete or unavailable Data Frame Layout documents, calibration drift) rather than a statistically representative frequency count across all FDR-related investigation delays.
- **The report does not state architectural passivity as a deliberate safety philosophy in so many words anywhere I read.** The one-way acquisition-to-recorder data path is described functionally (see Claim), inferable from the "Data Acquisition System" and "Acquisition unit" sections, but the report's own stated purpose is about *documentation and read-out quality for accident investigation*, not about articulating "the recorder must never become a control input" as a named design principle. This is worth flagging honestly: the document supports the architectural fact, not a stated design doctrine.
- **Much of the regulatory detail (JAR-OPS 1, JAA) is now historical**, having been superseded by EASA regulation in Europe since this report was written; the technical description of acquisition-unit architecture is durable, the specific compliance citations are dated.
